content: The study aimed to investigate the relationship between the proportion of energy derived from dietary fat and its effects on body weight and fatness in individuals not actively trying to lose weight. This was done by analyzing data from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and cohort studies involving adults, children, and young people. To conduct the research, databases such as CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL were searched up to specific dates in 2014, without language restrictions. Relevant references from prior reviews were also examined. The inclusion criteria for trials were strict: they had to be randomized intervention trials involving participants aged 24 months or older, comparing lower-fat diets to usual or moderate-fat diets without any intention of weight loss. The studies also needed to assess weight or body fatness after at least six months. Cohort studies were included if they evaluated the proportion of energy from fat at baseline and its relationship with body weight or fatness after at least one year. Decisions on study inclusion were made independently by multiple reviewers, with disagreements resolved through discussion or consultation with a third party. Data extraction was performed in duplicate to ensure accuracy, focusing on population characteristics, interventions, controls, and outcome measures. Weight and body fatness data were independently extracted at all available time points. Statistical analyses included random-effects meta-analyses, meta-regression, subgroup analyses, sensitivity analyses, and funnel plot assessments. The analysis included 32 RCTs with approximately 54,000 participants and data from 25 cohort studies. The RCTs consistently demonstrated a small but significant reduction in weight when participants consumed a lower proportion of energy from fat compared to a usual diet. This weight reduction was observed in nearly all included studies and remained robust across sensitivity analyses. On average, reducing fat intake led to a weight loss of 1.5 kg (95% confidence interval: -2.0 to -1.1 kg). Greater reductions in dietary fat were associated with greater weight loss. The effect on weight was stable over time and was accompanied by reductions in body mass index (BMI) (-0.5 kg/m², 95% CI: -0.7 to -0.3) and waist circumference (-0.3 cm, 95% CI: -0.6 to -0.02). In contrast, the cohort studies generally did not show a consistent relationship between total fat intake and subsequent measures of body weight, fatness, or changes in fatness. However, there was some evidence suggesting that lower fat intake was associated with smaller weight increases in middle-aged adults, but not in elderly adults. Similarly, in the highest-quality child cohort, lower fat intake was linked to smaller changes in BMI over time. In conclusion, RCTs demonstrated that reducing dietary fat intake, even without the intention to lose weight, resulted in modest but consistent reductions in body weight, BMI, and waist circumference. Greater reductions in fat intake and lower baseline fat consumption were associated with more pronounced weight loss. However, these findings were not consistently supported by cohort studies, which often failed to show a clear relationship between total fat intake and later measures of body fatness or changes in fatness across different age groups.
